messages:
alex: Quick question on flag scope resolution when we do canaries — if org=false, project=true, route unset, model=true, what’s the effective value? I thought specificity wins (route > model > project > org) but also remember some org-level guardrails should be able to block lower scopes. @maria @samira

maria: Short answer: specificity wins by default (route -> model -> project -> org). But there’s a separate "guardrail" attribute that can be set at org or project to force-deny. so two axes: precedence vs enforcement.

samira: +1. In practice we have two behaviors implemented: 1) normal overrides (most flags) and 2) enforced-deny (used for compliance/security flags). If org.enforce_deny == true then lower-level true does NOT override.

alex: OK that helps. So for my example (org=false, project=true, model=true) — if org.enforce_deny=false then model=true wins, app sees true. If org.enforce_deny=true then final=false. correct?

maria: Correct. Also note that route explicit settings beat model/project. Example order evaluated: check route scope -> model scope -> project scope -> org scope. The first explicit setting encountered (closest scope) is used unless an enforce_deny exists above.

tiago: small nuance: for multivariate canaries we evaluate audience rules at the route level before scope resolution. So you can have route-level canary audience that picks 5% and sets flag=true for those requests, while non-canary fall back to model/project/org resolution.

alex: Can we get a tiny pseudo-spec to reference in the rollout doc? I want to include in PR description.

maria: sure, paste this in the doc:```pseudo
# evaluate_flag(request, flag_name):
# 1) if any ancestor scope (org/project) has enforce_deny and its value == false -> return false
# 2) if route scope has explicit value -> return value
# 3) if model scope has explicit value -> return value
# 4) if project scope has explicit value -> return value
# 5) return org scope value (may be default)
```

samira: also add canary step up top: if route has canary_rule and request in canary -> return canary_value. so final becomes: canary -> enforce_deny check -> specificity scan.

alex: Perfect. A couple of ops questions: 1) who needs to be notified for the canary? 2) how long should canary run? 3) metrics/guardrails to watch?

maria: 1) ping release@, oncall (sre-oncall), and product lead. 2) baseline: 24h or 10k requests whichever comes first. 3) watch 5xx rate, tail latency (p99), and token cost delta. Thresholds: 5xx delta > 0.5% or p99 increase > 50% -> rollback.

tiago: also add model quality checks: run our regression eval suite for the canary prompts, expect >= 98% pass rate. If quality drops, fallback to stable model.

alex: Cool — for the PR I’ll include the pseudo-spec and rollout steps. Also will add a migration note to audit all org-level enforce_deny flags before enabling model-level overrides.

samira: one more: for UI/console we should surface enforce_deny with a red badge and tooltip "Blocks lower-scope enables" so PMs don’t accidentally flip it. Filing a tiny UX ticket now.

flagger-bot: NOTE: created flag-rollout/checklist #452 in backlog (link: https://redwood.internal/tickets/452)

alex: Thanks all — will draft the PR and tag you for review. cc @maria @samira

maria: lgtm, small nit: include example JSON for a route canary in the PR, e.g.:```json
{
  "flag": "new-rewrite",
  "scope": "route:payments/checkout",
  "canary": { "percent": 5, "value": true },
  "enforce_deny": false
}
```

alex: adding that now. will ping when ready.
